name: Jade Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brook End, which runs about six hundred sows indoors and four hundred acres of wheat and barley, and most of the barley goes back into the pig feed. I'm in the farrowing house, where the sows give birth, so my day is checking litters, moving piglets that aren't feeding, washing pens and writing everything down. I've been there eighteen months. Before that I did a bit of everything, bar work, warehouse, a year travelling.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the piglets that shouldn't make it and do. There was a runt last month I called Biscuit, I put her on a different sow three times, and she's fine now. What wears me down is the smell in my hair, the early starts, and the fact that I'm still slower than Gail at everything, even washing a pen.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time. I use one to check symptoms before I bother the vet, one to turn my scribbled notes into the weekly report, and I've been playing with an app that counts piglets from a phone photo. Gail, my supervisor, rolls her eyes but she's started asking me to look things up for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's brilliant and we're not using it nearly enough. I'd probably post a video of the piglet counter, because it's honestly very cool. My mates who work in offices think pig farming is from the middle ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it makes me more useful than my hands do right now. I'm slow in the pens, but I'm the one who can get the report done in ten minutes. That buys me some time to get better at the real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager, Mr Okafor, if we can trial the piglet counter properly for a month and compare it with Gail's counts. I'd do an online course in pig health, there's a cheap one I've been eyeing. And I'd keep my savings where they are, they're doing fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. It's the version where I get to tinker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the savings.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lived with my mum till I was twenty-five and saved almost everything from the warehouse job, which paid nights. So I've got about a year and a half of wages put by. My girlfriend Priya calls it my bunker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Gail go along with a trial against her counts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd pretend not to care and then check every single number. Which is fine, because that's exactly what a trial should be. She's been doing it twenty years and she's usually right.

S0.say: I'd say it's brilliant and we're not using it nearly enough. I'd post a video of the piglet counter to show office friends that pig farming isn't from the middle ages.
S0.think: I think it makes me more useful than my hands do right now. I'm slow in the pens but fast with reports, and that buys me time to get better at the real work.
S0.do: Asks Mr Okafor for a month's trial of the piglet counter compared against Gail's counts. Takes a cheap online pig health course and leaves her savings alone.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit excited, since this is the version where she gets to tinker.
S0.quote: I'm slow in the pens, but I'm the one who can get the report done in ten minutes.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is cheerful and frank that her worth on the farm is currently her tech skill, not her stockwork. Her savings came from night shifts and living at home, and her partner calls them her bunker. She respects Gail's experience even while wanting to test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's bad news for people starting out, and that firms should be made to keep taking on apprentices. Somebody gave me a go with no farm background at all. I'd want that for the next person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's fine for me, because I'd be the one who knows the tools. But I'd feel a bit like I'd climbed in through a window just before they locked it. And I'd worry the farm only ever hires people who already know everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the person who trains any new starters on the tech. I'd push Mr Okafor to keep one apprentice place a year, and offer to mentor them myself. And I'd start the pig health course properly, not just eye it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of whoever comes after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a beginner at Brook End now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Kieran, he's nineteen, on the arable side. He drives the grain trailer and he's terrified of the pigs. If they'd stopped hiring beginners, he'd still be stacking shelves in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're keen on the tools. Is there anything you wouldn't hand over to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deciding when a sow needs help. Gail knows from how a sow's lying, before anything shows on a screen. I'm nowhere near that, and I'd hate a tool to stop me ever learning it.

S1.say: I'd say it's bad news for people starting out and that firms should have to keep taking apprentices. Somebody gave me a go with no farm background, and I'd want that for the next person.
S1.think: I think I'm fine because I know the tools, but it feels like climbing in a window just before it's locked. I'd worry the farm only hires people who already know everything.
S1.do: Offers to train new starters on the tech and pushes Mr Okafor to keep one apprentice place a year that she'd mentor. Starts the pig health course for real.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly for whoever comes after her.
S1.quote: I'd feel a bit like I'd climbed in through a window just before they locked it.
S1.fieldNote: Her progressive views show up as concern for the next beginner, with Kieran as the real example. She draws a clear line at handing over the judgement of when a sow needs help. Notable for an AI enthusiast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people losing office jobs need proper support, and the companies making the AI should pay for it. I'd say the new AI jobs should go to the people who lost the old ones, with training paid for. I'd be loud about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly good for me. Farm records, ordering, compliance forms, all of it gets done by an assistant, and I'm the person who sets it up and checks it. But Priya works in a call centre for an energy company, and she'd be right in the firing line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mr Okafor about letting me set up an AI assistant for all the farm paperwork, and maybe ask for a pay rise to match. I'd sit down with Priya and go through which of the new jobs she could go for. We'd agree she can stop work for six months if she needs to retrain, on my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for me and worried for Priya, which is a weird thing to feel in the same evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the bunker's for both of us, not just me. Then I'd probably make her look at job ads with me until midnight, which she'd hate. She'd say I treat everything like a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be setting up the thing that takes paperwork off people. Does that sit right with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, because on our farm nobody's job is paperwork, it's an extra on top. But if I were doing it at the feed company, I'd feel different. I'd want the people it replaced to get something, not just me getting a raise.

S2.say: I'd say people losing office jobs need proper support paid for by the AI companies. The new AI jobs should go to those who lost the old ones, with training paid for, and I'd be loud about it online.
S2.think: I think it's mostly good for me, because I'd set up and check the farm's paperwork assistant. But my girlfriend works in an energy company call centre and would be right in the firing line.
S2.do: Asks Mr Okafor to let her set up an AI assistant for the farm paperwork, with a pay rise to match. Goes through the new jobs with Priya and offers her six months off to retrain, funded from savings.
S2.feel: Excited for herself and worried for Priya in the same evening.
S2.quote: I'd tell her the bunker's for both of us, not just me.
S2.fieldNote: She sees herself gaining here and admits it plainly. When asked whether her role sits with her politics, she drew a careful line between adding a tool and replacing a person. Her savings become shared household insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a proper fight over who gets the gains, through taxes on shares and property. I'd go on every march, honestly. If houses boom while people are thrown out of work, that's broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in a funny spot. My job is safe because it's physical, and I've got savings, so I'm not hurting. But Priya probably loses her job in this one, and we'd never buy a house at those prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the savings in cash and not chase the boom, because it would feel wrong and I don't trust it. I'd ask Mr Okafor about a supervisor track, since my job's one of the safe ones now and I want to be good at it. And I'd help Priya look at farm work too, maybe on the arable side with Kieran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry about the politics, safe about my job, and sad about the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Priya actually work on a farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says she'd rather die than smell like I do. But she'd do the grain side, I reckon, driving and sampling. She's careful and she reads instructions, which is more than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't chase the boom. Not even a bit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a tiny bit, if I'm really honest. My mum would tell me to buy shares, and she's usually right about money. But I'd feel like I was cheering for the thing that sacked my girlfriend.

S3.say: I'd say this is the moment to fight over who gets the gains, through taxes on shares and property. I'd join every march, because a house boom while people lose work is broken.
S3.think: I think I'm in a funny spot: my physical job is safe and I've got savings. But Priya probably loses her job, and we'd never afford a house at boom prices.
S3.do: Keeps savings in cash rather than chasing the boom, and asks Mr Okafor about a supervisor track. Helps Priya look at arable farm work on the grain side.
S3.feel: Angry about the politics, safe about her job and sad about the house.
S3.quote: I'd feel like I was cheering for the thing that sacked my girlfriend.
S3.fieldNote: When pushed, she admitted she might buy a few shares after all, then explained why she'd feel bad about it. Her own position is strong, but her household's isn't. Priya's possible move to the grain side was a nice, specific idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots should be partly owned by the workers or the public, not just the company that built them. Something like the farm owning one share and the people it replaced owning another. I'd say that everywhere, and I'd join whatever union was fighting for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd want to be the person running them. Pig sheds are hot, wet and dirty, and I'd be glad if a robot washed pens instead of me. There are eleven of us at Brook End. I'd rather be the person who fixes the robot than the person it replaced, but I know that's not a job for all eleven of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask the dealer or the company for training, and pay for it myself out of savings if the farm won't. I'd go to Mr Okafor with a plan: robots wash and feed, people do the stockwork, nobody gets sacked for two years. And I'd push the union hard on a deal for retraining, because I can't be the only one who comes out fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty. I'd love the robots and hate what they'd do to Gail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she's the one who knows when a sow's in trouble, and no robot I've seen can do that. I'd half believe it. She'd say, you'll be fine, you're the robot girl, and she'd be right, which is the worst bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever not take the robot job, if it meant others lost theirs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it, and no, I'd take it. If I don't, someone from the robot company does, and they won't care about Biscuit or Kieran. I'd rather be in the room and fighting for the others from inside.

S4.say: I'd say robots should be partly owned by workers or the public, not just the company that built them. I'd push for that everywhere and join any union fighting for it.
S4.think: I'd want to be the one running the robots, since pig sheds are hot and dirty work. But there are eleven of us at Brook End, and a robot doesn't need eleven minders.
S4.do: Seeks robot training in the first month, paying from savings if the farm won't. Pitches Mr Okafor a plan where robots wash and feed, people do stockwork and no one is sacked for two years, and pushes the union on retraining.
S4.feel: Excited and guilty, loving the robots but hating what they'd do to Gail.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the person who fixes the robot than the person it replaced, but I know that's not a job for all eleven of us.
S4.fieldNote: Jade is the rare one who'd welcome robots for herself, and she's honest that she'd take the job even if others lost theirs. Her plan for a two-year no-sacking period was specific. Her worry is entirely for Gail and the others, and the guilt felt real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, but not for me, for everyone else at Brook End. I'll be fine, I'm the robot girl. What would help is a law that says when a farm brings in robots, it has to fund training for the people there and keep them on for a while, and some share of the robots going to the workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs. Nobody asks whether a sow does better or worse with a robot washing her pen, and I honestly don't know.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the person who fixes the robot than the person it replaced, but I know that's not a job for all eleven of us.
portrait: Jade is a 27-year-old junior in the farrowing house of a pig and arable farm who saved hard on warehouse night shifts and now has about a year and a half of wages put by. She uses AI daily, is slow in the pens but quick with the tech, and sees each picture as a chance to be useful, while worrying about beginners like Kieran, her girlfriend Priya in a call centre, and her supervisor Gail. Her progressive politics lead her to argue for worker or public ownership of robots. In the robot picture she'd take the robot job without hesitation and fight for the others from inside, and she feels guilty about it.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, not for herself but for her co-workers at the pig farm, especially Gail.
whatWouldHelp: A law making farms that bring in robots fund training and keep staff on for a while, plus a share of the robots going to workers.
